description: DynamicDuo is an ambitious, high-impact team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.
summary:
Flame in Freefall is an interactive web dashboard that helps researchers and engineers quickly understand and prioritize NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments for real crew environments.

The tool ranks investigations such as BASS-II, Saffire, FLEX, ACME, and SAME against target conditions for lunar bases, pressurized rovers, the ISS, and deep-space capsules. Ranking is based on oxygen concentration, cabin pressure, airflow, and safety pillars (prevention, detection, and suppression). Users can compare experiments side-by-side, search NASA NTRS documents with source citations, and run a machine-learning prediction trained on real FLEX droplet-combustion data to estimate extinction probability and burn rate.

By turning decades of scattered PSI and NTRS data into clear, ranked, and interpretable insights, the dashboard supports better material selection, fire-detection design, and suppression strategies for future Moon and Mars missions. All results are linked back to original NASA sources and are intended as decision support only.
details:
We built Flame in Freefall, an interactive dashboard that makes NASA’s microgravity combustion data easier to find, compare, and use for real crew environments.

We collected and cleaned experimental data from NASA’s Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database, focusing on investigations such as BASS-II, Saffire, FLEX, ACME, SAME, and others. We also gathered relevant NASA NTRS technical reports and extracted key information about objectives, fuels, oxygen levels, pressure, airflow, sensors, and safety pillars.

We created a ranking system that scores each investigation against different target environments (Lunar Base, Pressurized Rover, ISS, and Orion capsule). The ranking looks at how well the tested conditions match the needs of each environment, especially oxygen concentration, cabin pressure, and airflow. We added a side-by-side comparison view so users can quickly see similarities and differences between experiments.

We trained a machine-learning model on cleaned FLEX droplet-combustion data to predict extinction probability and burn rate. We also built a search feature that lets users ask questions and get matching passages directly from the NASA documents, with file and page citations.

The frontend was developed with React and Vite, and the backend with FastAPI. Everything runs on publicly available NASA data. Our goal was to turn decades of scattered research into clear, ranked insights that can help engineers and researchers working on fire safety for future Moon and Mars missions. The tool is meant as decision support only and does not replace official testing or NASA standards.
